university: University of Texas at El Paso

documents.title: UTEP Guidance for Teaching with AI Technologies (Fall 2025: Teaching and Learning in an AI World)
documents.stance_why: The guide says faculty may 'fully embrace AI in your course, allow limited use, or prohibit it altogether' and supplies five sample statements (Free Use, Permitted with Acknowledgement, Brainstorming or Early Stages, Allowed with Permission, Not Permitted). It sets no single university rule and hands the decision to instructors with tiers, so the stance is delegates.
tiers: AI for Brainstorming or Early Stages
documents.summary: Provost guidance asks UTEP faculty to choose their own AI stance, explain it to students, and set clear boundaries, with five sample syllabus statements from free use to a ban. It stresses student responsibility, transparency and ethical use, and refers misuse to Community Standards under existing integrity policy. A closing conversation-starter list gives students seven habits for responsible use.

units.why: The opening tells faculty they may 'fully embrace AI in your course, allow limited use, or prohibit it altogether', so the decision is left to each instructor. P04 fits because the choice is per course; it informs rather than commands.
units.anchor: allow limited use, or prohibit it altogether

units.why: Faculty are told to 'communicate your rationale clearly' and 'establish fair and transparent boundaries'. This asks instructors to explain the reasons behind their rules, so P66 fits better than P09, which would require a syllabus statement and this does not.
units.anchor: communicate your rationale
units.policy: Instructors communicate their rationale for their AI stance clearly.

units.why: The guidance offers 'ready-to-use syllabus language, guiding questions, and adaptable frameworks', which is the institution supplying templates for instructors (P110).
units.anchor: ready-to-use syllabus language, guiding questions, and adaptable frameworks

units.why: States 'we encourage faculty to integrate Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies thoughtfully and transparently'. It is encouragement of AI use, so P02 is the nearest type, but it is addressed to faculty integrating AI in teaching rather than to student use.
units.anchor: we encourage faculty to
units.policy: UTEP encourages faculty to integrate AI technologies thoughtfully and transparently into teaching and learning.
units.fit_note: Encouragement addressed to faculty integrating AI in teaching, not a rule for student use.

units.why: 'AI tools can enrich the classroom when used to enhance—not replace—student thinking' sets the condition for good AI use: AI must not replace the student's thinking, which is P32.
units.anchor: enhance—not replace—student thinking, creativity, and ownership of learning
units.frag_start: AI tools can enrich the classroom

units.why: Regardless of approach, faculty must 'Communicate your rationale governing your AI stance clearly. Share the "why" with students.' This is an explicit duty to give students the reasons for the rules, P66.
units.anchor: Share the “why” with students.

units.why: 'Establish fair and transparent boundaries' tells instructors to set clear and fair limits on AI. P124 (apply rules consistently and transparently) is the nearest type.
units.anchor: Establish fair and transparent boundaries.
units.fit_note: Asks for fair and transparent boundaries when they are set, not consistent application across students.

units.why: Faculty should 'foster student ownership of learning' by 'cultivating reflective and iterative practices'. This asks for reflective assignment design, so P35 (redesign assignments around AI) is the nearest type.
units.anchor: cultivating reflective and iterative practices that challenge students
units.policy: Instructors foster student ownership of learning in an AI-enhanced world by cultivating reflective and iterative practices that challenge students to think deeply about their processes.
units.fit_note: Reflective practice is a general pedagogical aim, not a specific redesign.

units.why: Prompts instructors to ask 'How does my stance on AI align with my course learning outcomes?', tying the AI decision to learning objectives (P83).
units.anchor: How does my stance on AI align with my course learning outcomes?
units.frag_start: How does my stance on AI

units.why: The question 'How might I turn my AI policy into a learning conversation rather than a restriction?' asks instructors to discuss AI with students instead of only restricting it; P66.
units.anchor: turn my AI policy into a learning conversation rather than a restriction?

units.why: Asks 'What scaffolds (practice, reflection, citation) can I add to make AI use transparent', suggesting instructors add reflection and citation to assignments. P35 covers assignment redesign.
units.anchor: What scaffolds (practice, reflection, citation) can I add

units.why: 'This isn't about surveillance! The goal is not to "catch" AI misuse' says staff aim to cultivate responsible use rather than police it; P60 (decline to police) is the nearest fit.
units.anchor: The goal is not to “catch” AI misuse
units.fit_note: Does not rule out enforcement; it frames the purpose as cultivating responsible use.

units.why: 'Clear expectations reduce confusion and help students develop discernment' explains why expectations are stated. It is closest to P99 (easing causes of misuse), but only loosely, since confusion is not a pressure such as a deadline.
units.anchor: Clear expectations reduce confusion
units.fit_note: Reduces confusion, not pressure such as deadlines; weak fit.

units.why: Instructors should 'Model curiosity and critical evaluation' to show 'when to seek assistance, when to question results'. This is instructors modelling responsible AI use, P112.
units.anchor: Model curiosity and critical evaluation

units.why: 'the resulting grade will belong to the student, not the AI program' says students are responsible for whatever they submit, including AI errors. P29.
units.anchor: the resulting grade will belong to the student, not the AI program
units.policy: Instructors impress upon students that if they put their name on an assignment they take complete responsibility for its content, and that the grade belongs to the student, not the AI program, if AI content is flawed.

units.why: 'Remind students that AI cannot reproduce critical thought, reflection, or personal insights' tells instructors to relay that AI does not replace human thinking, closest to P32.
units.anchor: AI cannot reproduce critical thought, reflection, or personal insights.
units.fit_note: A statement of AI's limits for instructors to relay, not a rule for student behavior.

units.why: Instructors are told to 'Discuss with students the ethical as well as practical ramifications of using falsified information and references, which generative AI content often includes'. AI output is often wrong and must be checked: P31.
units.anchor: falsified information and references, which generative AI content

units.why: 'outline what constitutes AI misuse in your course and ... make clear the consequences' asks instructors to say how misuse is defined and handled, P123.
units.anchor: outline what constitutes AI misuse in your course
units.policy: Instructors outline what constitutes AI misuse in their course and make clear the consequences of crossing those boundaries.

units.why: 'Define which assignments or process stages explicitly prohibit AI use' tells instructors to mark per-assignment bans, so the rule is set per assignment (P04).
units.anchor: Define which assignments or process stages explicitly prohibit AI use.

units.why: 'Clarify that violations fall under UTEP's existing academic integrity policies' classifies AI violations under existing integrity rules, P36.
units.anchor: violations fall under UTEP’s existing academic integrity policies.

units.why: 'academic misuse of AI will be directed to the Office of Community Standards' sets the referral route for misuse, a formal reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: academic misuse of AI will be directed to the Office of Community Standards.
units.fit_note: Names the office misuse goes to; procedural steps are not given.

units.why: Sample statement 'Free Use of AI': 'AI use is freely permitted in this class. You are encouraged to explore creative, responsible, and ethical ways to use AI.' It is the open tier of five named options, so P05 is chosen over P02 because it is offered as one tier.
units.anchor: AI use is freely permitted in this class.
units.fit_note: Also P02 content (free use encouraged); filed under the tier framework.

units.why: Sample 'AI Use Permitted with Acknowledgement': 'you must describe and acknowledge how you used them with each submission', a disclosure duty with every submission, P24.
units.anchor: you must describe and acknowledge how you used them with each submission.

units.why: The same statement says 'Any uncredited AI-generated content will be treated as plagiarism', making nondisclosure the violation (P28).
units.anchor: Any uncredited AI-generated content will be treated as plagiarism

units.why: Sample 'AI for Brainstorming or Early Stages': 'You may use AI tools to brainstorm ideas or plan your approach', a narrow permitted use, P15.
units.anchor: You may use AI tools to brainstorm ideas or plan your approach.

units.why: 'your final work must reflect your own reasoning and analysis' requires submitted work to be the student's own thinking, P29.
units.anchor: your final work must reflect your own reasoning and analysis.

units.why: 'AI-generated ideas are not your own and must be cited if directly included' requires citation of AI ideas that are included, P24.
units.anchor: AI-generated ideas are not your own and must be cited if directly included.

units.why: Sample 'AI Allowed with Permission': 'You may use AI tools only with prior instructor approval', permission required first, P107.
units.anchor: You may use AI tools only with prior instructor approval.

units.why: Under the permission tier, 'include a brief note in your submission describing how you used the tool and cite the tool properly' requires disclosure and citation of the tool, P25.
units.anchor: include a brief note in your submission describing how you used the tool
units.fit_note: Asks for a note on use and proper tool citation; no prompt or date is required.

units.why: Sample 'AI Use Not Permitted': 'Use of AI technologies is not permitted in this course', a course-level ban, P01.
units.anchor: Use of AI technologies is not permitted in this course.

units.why: 'This policy ensures that your work demonstrates your own learning and critical thinking' gives the reason for a ban: the work must show the student's own learning, P41.
units.anchor: your work demonstrates your own learning and critical thinking.

units.why: 'Any identified AI-generated content will be treated as plagiarism and referred to the Office of Community Standards' under the ban classifies prohibited AI use as plagiarism, P36.
units.anchor: Any identified AI-generated content will be treated as plagiarism

units.why: Points faculty to a Vanderbilt compilation of syllabus statements: 'For more examples, please see this resource', P115.
units.anchor: For more examples, please see this resource from Vanderbilt University

units.why: 'Students are more likely to respect AI boundaries when they understand why those boundaries exist' explains why rationale should be shared, P66.
units.anchor: Students are more likely to respect AI boundaries when they understand why

units.why: 'When you introduce your AI policy, pair it with your learning goals for the assignment and express your rationale' directs assignment-level explanation. P66 chosen since the instruction is to explain; P04 does not fit as it does not say who decides.
units.anchor: pair it with your learning goals for the assignment and express your rationale.
units.frag_start: When you introduce your AI policy,

units.why: 'Yes, and here's how': 'AI may be used freely with transparent acknowledgement, documentation of prompts and prompt evolution, and a reflective evaluation'. An open tier whose condition is documented prompts and reflection, so P26.
units.anchor: documentation of prompts and prompt evolution, and a reflective evaluation
units.frag_start: AI may be used freely with
units.policy: AI may be used freely with transparent acknowledgement, documentation of prompts and prompt evolution, and a reflective evaluation of the output and the student's revisions to it.
units.fit_note: Combines free use with acknowledgement and reflection.

units.why: 'Sometimes, and here's when': 'AI may be used in specific stages of course projects: brainstorming, outlining, and editing', a limited list of uses, P107.
units.anchor: AI may be used in specific stages of course projects: brainstorming, outlining, and editing.
units.fit_note: Limits AI to named project stages.

units.why: 'No, and here's why': 'AI use is not permitted because it would prevent you from practicing _______ skill' bans AI where it blocks skill practice, P41.
units.anchor: AI use is not permitted because it would prevent you from practicing
units.fit_note: A ban with its reason built in.

units.why: The three guiding statements are called a framework that 'promotes transparency, fairness, and student judgment': a named three-way categorisation of AI use, P05.
units.anchor: This framework, borrowed from Jeffrey Washburn
units.policy: The yes/sometimes/no framework, borrowed from Jeffrey Washburn (UT Permian Basin), promotes transparency, fairness, and student judgment.

units.why: 'it's our responsibility to help students engage with these technologies ethically, transparently, and with critical judgment' is a general call for ethical use, P116.
units.anchor: it’s our responsibility to help students engage with these technologies ethically

units.why: AI tools 'are becoming integral to academic, professional, and creative environments' frames AI as part of professional life, the career reason for teaching AI use, P44.
units.anchor: AI-powered tools are becoming integral to academic, professional, and creative environments.

units.why: Principles help students 'Recognize how AI can support—not replace—human thought, creativity, and collaboration', again AI must not replace thinking, P32.
units.anchor: Recognize how AI can support—not replace—human thought, creativity, and collaboration

units.why: 'Make intentional choices about when and how to engage with AI' asks students to decide deliberately whether to use AI. P118 (weigh benefits, risks, values) is nearest.
units.anchor: Make intentional choices about when and how to engage with AI
units.fit_note: Intentional choice, but benefits and risks are not named.

units.why: Section 2 repeats the responsibility bullets of section 1 (coded once above); the distinct sentence here is 'AI is only a tool to be used, but it does not replace human intellect', closest to P32.
units.anchor: AI is only a tool to be used, but it does not replace human intellect
units.frag_start: Discuss with your students that AI

units.why: Conversation starter 1, 'Use AI to learn, not to shortcut learning': AI can support 'brainstorming, outlining, or clarifying', but the student's reasoning must drive the work. The student stays the primary thinker, P32.
units.anchor: your ideas, voice, and
units.frag_start: AI tools can support brainstorming, outlining, or clarifying
units.policy: Students use AI to learn, not to shortcut learning; AI tools can support brainstorming, outlining, or clarifying, but the student's ideas, voice, and reasoning must drive the work.

units.why: Conversation starter 2: 'Be transparent about your use' and follow the instructor's guidelines on citing or disclosing, P24.
units.anchor: Be transparent about your use

units.why: Conversation starter 3: 'Always fact-check, cross-reference, and apply your own judgment' to AI output, P31.
units.anchor: Always fact-check, cross-reference, and apply

units.why: Conversation starter 4: 'Don't pass off AI-generated content as your original work unless allowed', P19.
units.anchor: Don’t pass off AI-generated content as your original work unless allowed.

units.why: Conversation starter 5: 'Follow the ground rules of each assignment. Some course activities may prohibit AI use', students follow each assignment's rules, P78.
units.anchor: Some course activities may prohibit AI use to develop your critical thinking
units.policy: Students follow the ground rules of each assignment; some course activities may prohibit AI use to develop critical thinking or communication skills, and students respect those boundaries.

units.why: Conversation starter 6: 'Struggle and reflection are part of developing mastery', the skill-building reason for not overriding the learning process with AI, P41.
units.anchor: Struggle and reflection are part of developing mastery.

units.why: Conversation starter 7: 'Avoid entering personal, sensitive, or proprietary information into AI tools', P50.
units.anchor: Avoid entering personal, sensitive, or proprietary information into AI tools.

units.why: Starter 7 also says 'Know what happens to your input', warning that tools may keep what is entered, P50.
units.anchor: Know what happens to your input.

notes: Only one included document. Section 2 of the guide repeats the personal-responsibility bullets from section 1; coded once. P66 was used rather than P09 because the guide does not require a syllabus statement.
